  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsection"><a href="#S5.SS5" title="In 5 Results ‣ Leap+Verify: Regime-Adaptive Speculative Weight Predictionfor Accelerating Neural Network Training" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">5.5 </span>Cascade Evaluation</span></a></li>
</ol></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_section"><a href="#S6" title="In Leap+Verify: Regime-Adaptive Speculative Weight Predictionfor Accelerating Neural Network Training" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">6 </span>Discussion</span></a>
<ol class="ltx_toclist ltx_toclist_section">
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsection"><a href="#S6.SS1" title="In 6 Discussion ‣ Leap+Verify: Regime-Adaptive Speculative Weight Predictionfor Accelerating Neural Network Training" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">6.1 </span>The Universal Momentum Catastrophe</span></a></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsection"><a href="#S6.SS2" title="In 6 Discussion ‣ Leap+Verify: Regime-Adaptive Speculative Weight Predictionfor Accelerating Neural Network Training" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">6.2 </span>Scale-Dependent Regime Distribution</span></a></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsection"><a href="#S6.SS3" title="In 6 Discussion ‣ Leap+Verify: Regime-Adaptive Speculative Weight Predictionfor Accelerating Neural Network Training" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">6.3 </span>Regime Detection as a Prerequisite for Prediction</span></a></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsection"><a href="#S6.SS4" title="In 6 Discussion ‣ Leap+Verify: Regime-Adaptive Speculative Weight Predictionfor Accelerating Neural Network Training" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">6.4 </span>Connection to ASC</span></a></li>

</ol></li>

<div class="ltx_page_main">
<div id="infobox" class="infobox">

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Leap+Verify: Regime-Adaptive Speculative Weight Prediction
<br class="ltx_break">for Accelerating Neural Network Training</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Jeremy McEntire
</span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Leap+Verify</span>, a framework that applies speculative execution—predicting future model weights and validating predictions before acceptance—to accelerate neural network training.
Inspired by speculative decoding in language model inference and by the Automatically Scalable Computation (ASC) architecture for program execution, Leap+Verify decomposes training into three dynamically detected regimes (chaotic, transition, stable) using activation-space cosine similarity as a real-time Lyapunov proxy signal.
Within each regime, analytic weight predictors (momentum, linear, quadratic extrapolation) attempt to forecast model parameters <math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> training steps ahead; predictions are accepted only when validated against a held-out loss criterion.</p>
    
<p id="abstract1.2" class="ltx_p">We evaluate Leap+Verify on GPT-2 124M and Qwen 2.5-1.5B trained on WikiText-103 across five random seeds, sweeping prediction depth <math id="abstract1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K\in\{5,10,25,50,75,100\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>25</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>50</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>75</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K\in\{5,10,25,50,75,100\}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Momentum-based prediction (Adam moment extrapolation) fails catastrophically at <em id="abstract1.2.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">both</em> scales, with predicted losses exceeding actuals by <math id="abstract1.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="100{-}10{,}000\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>100</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>10,000</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">100{-}10{,}000\times</annotation></semantics></math>—a universal <span id="abstract1.2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">norm explosion</span> in optimizer-state extrapolation.
Finite-difference predictors (linear, quadratic) succeed where momentum fails: at 124M, they achieve 24% strict acceptance at <math id="abstract1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K{=}5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K{=}5</annotation></semantics></math> in stable regimes; at 1.5B, they achieve 37% strict acceptance in transition regimes.
The <span id="abstract1.2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">scale-dependent</span> finding is in regime distribution: GPT-2 124M spends 34% of training in stable regime, while Qwen 1.5B spends 64% in chaotic regime and reaches stable in only 0–2 of 40 checkpoints.
Larger models are <em id="abstract1.2.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">more predictable when predictable</em>, but <em id="abstract1.2.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">less often predictable</em>—the practical bottleneck shifts from predictor accuracy to regime availability.
Cross-seed results are highly consistent (<math id="abstract1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&lt;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>&lt;</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&lt;</annotation></semantics></math>1% validation loss variance), and the three-regime framework produces identical phase boundaries (<math id="abstract1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm 50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>±</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm 50</annotation></semantics></math> steps) across seeds.</p>
  
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Training modern neural networks is an inherently sequential process: each gradient update depends on the current parameter state, which depends on all prior updates.
This sequential bottleneck consumes enormous computational resources—training frontier language models requires thousands of GPU-hours and millions of dollars <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kaplan et al., 2020</a>)</cite>.
Yet the sequential nature of gradient descent is not as rigid as it appears.
Weight trajectories exhibit substantial regularity, particularly in late training, suggesting that future parameter states may be predictable from past trajectory information.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Speculative execution</span> offers a principled way to exploit such predictability.
In speculative decoding for language model inference <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Leviathan et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, a small draft model generates candidate tokens that the target model verifies in parallel, achieving 2–3<math id="S1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> speedup without altering the output distribution.
The key insight is the <em id="S1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">verify-then-accept</em> mechanism: predictions are cheap to generate and cheap to validate, so even moderate prediction accuracy yields substantial speedup.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We transplant this mechanism from inference to training.
<span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Leap+Verify</span> predicts future model weights <math id="S1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> steps ahead using analytic extrapolation of the weight trajectory, then validates the predicted weights against a held-out loss criterion before accepting the advance.
The name derives from the Automatically Scalable Computation (ASC) architecture <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Waterland et al., 2014</a>)</cite>, which accelerates sequential program execution by speculatively predicting future program states and caching verified state transitions.
In ASC, a <em id="S1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">recognizer</em> identifies predictable states, <em id="S1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">predictors</em> forecast future states, and a <em id="S1.p3.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">validator</em> confirms correctness before fast-forwarding execution.
Leap+Verify instantiates each component for neural network training: the recognizer is an activation-space regime detector, the predictors are analytic weight extrapolators, and the validator is a held-out loss comparison.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">A central finding is that prediction viability depends critically on the <em id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">training regime</em>.
We identify three regimes—chaotic, transition, and stable—using cosine similarity between consecutive activation fingerprints as a proxy for the local Lyapunov exponent.
Prediction is viable only in transition and stable regimes, where weight trajectories exhibit sufficient regularity.
This regime dependence motivates <em id="S1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">conditional</em> prediction: the system predicts only when the regime detector indicates favorable conditions, avoiding wasted computation during chaotic training phases.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Our most striking empirical finding is a <span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">universal momentum catastrophe</span>: Adam moment extrapolation produces weight predictions <math id="S1.p5.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="100{-}10{,}000\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>100</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>10,000</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">100{-}10{,}000\times</annotation></semantics></math> worse than actual validation loss at both 124M and 1.5B parameters.
This catastrophe is caused by norm explosion—the extrapolated displacement <math id="S1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K\cdot m_{t}/\sqrt{v_{t}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>/</mo><msqrt><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K\cdot m_{t}/\sqrt{v_{t}}</annotation></semantics></math> far exceeds the region of validity around the current point on the loss surface.
Finite-difference predictors (linear, quadratic), which extrapolate from actually observed checkpoint deltas, avoid this failure and achieve 9–37% strict acceptance at <math id="S1.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K{=}5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K{=}5</annotation></semantics></math> depending on regime and scale, with proximity-based acceptance reaching 100% at short horizons.
The <span id="S1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">scale-dependent</span> finding is that the distribution of training regimes shifts dramatically: at 1.5B, training remains chaotic for 64% of checkpoints (vs. 4% at 124M), severely limiting when prediction is viable.
This regime-availability bottleneck has not been identified in prior work on weight nowcasting <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jang and Han, 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Knyazev et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guan et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Contributions.</h4>

<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<ol id="S1.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Leap+Verify</span>: A verify-then-accept mechanism for speculative weight prediction during training, inspired by speculative decoding and ASC.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Regime-conditional prediction</span>: Three dynamically detected training regimes (chaotic, transition, stable) that determine when and how to predict.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Universal momentum catastrophe and scale-dependent regime distribution</span>: Empirical demonstration that optimizer-state extrapolation fails at all scales, while the regime availability bottleneck grows with model size.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">4.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Reproducible evaluation</span>: Five-seed experiments with consistent results across GPT-2 124M and Qwen 2.5-1.5B on WikiText-103.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Background and Motivation</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Automatically Scalable Computation</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The Automatically Scalable Computation (ASC) architecture <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Waterland et al., 2014</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Waterland et al., 2013</a>)</cite> accelerates sequential program execution by viewing it as a trajectory through state space.
The architecture has three core components: (1) a <em id="S2.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">recognizer</em> that identifies states amenable to prediction, (2) a set of <em id="S2.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">predictors</em> that learn to forecast future states from observed trajectory structure, and (3) a <em id="S2.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">trajectory cache</em> that stores verified start-state/end-state pairs for fast-forwarding.
When the recognizer identifies a predictable state, predictors generate candidate future states, speculative threads execute from those candidates, and results are cached.
The sequential execution thread periodically queries the cache; on a match, it fast-forwards to the cached end state, achieving speedup proportional to prediction accuracy and trajectory length <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Waterland et al., 2014</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">ASC was originally implemented for x86 binary programs, where state vectors represent processor registers and memory.
The present work adapts the architecture for neural network training, where the “state vector” is the model’s parameter tensor and the “transition function” is a gradient update step.
The exponentially large state space of parameters becomes tractable because training trajectories, like program trajectories, exhibit regular structure that predictors can exploit.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Speculative Decoding</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Speculative decoding <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Leviathan et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Stern et al., 2018</a>)</cite> accelerates autoregressive language model inference by using a small draft model to generate candidate token sequences that the target model verifies in parallel.
The critical property is that verification is cheaper than generation: checking whether a sequence of <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> tokens is acceptable requires a single forward pass, while generating them sequentially requires <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> passes.
Acceptance is governed by a rejection sampling scheme that preserves the target distribution exactly.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Leap+Verify adapts the predict-then-verify template to training.
The “draft model” is an analytic weight extrapolator (momentum, linear, or quadratic); the “verification” is a loss evaluation on held-out data.
Unlike speculative decoding, where acceptance is binary and distribution-preserving, Leap+Verify uses graded acceptance criteria (strict, adaptive, proximity-based) that trade off between conservatism and skip distance.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>Training Dynamics and Phase Transitions</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Neural network training traverses qualitatively different regimes.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cohen et al. (2021)</a></cite> identified two phases in full-batch gradient descent: progressive sharpening (where the maximum Hessian eigenvalue rises to <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2/\eta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>/</mo><mi>η</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2/\eta</annotation></semantics></math>) and edge-of-stability (where sharpness oscillates at this threshold).
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lewkowycz et al. (2020)</a></cite> documented a “catapult phase” where loss temporarily grows before decreasing.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Frankle et al. (2020)</a></cite> showed that networks become “stable to SGD noise” early in training, after which models sharing a common training prefix converge to linearly connected solutions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">These observations suggest a multi-phase training structure, but prior work detects phases using expensive Hessian computations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cohen et al., 2021</a>)</cite> or post-hoc weight-space analysis <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Frankle et al., 2020</a>)</cite>.
We use activation-space cosine similarity as an efficient, real-time proxy that requires only forward passes on a fixed probe set.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.4 </span>Weight Nowcasting</h3>

<div id="S2.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Several lines of work predict future weights during training.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kamarthi and Pittner (1999)</a></cite> used Taylor series extrapolation of weight trajectories.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sinha et al. (2017)</a></cite> trained a neural network to forecast future weights from weight history.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jang and Han (2023)</a></cite> designed the Weight Nowcaster Network (WNN), predicting 5 epochs ahead from 5 epochs of history.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Knyazev et al. (2025)</a></cite> improved this with graph neural networks modeling neuron connectivity (NiNo), achieving up to 50% training acceleration.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guan et al. (2024)</a></cite> proposed XGrad, predicting future weights using optimizer update rules.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">All existing weight prediction methods apply predictions <em id="S2.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">unconditionally</em>—they do not verify predictions before acceptance, and they do not condition on detected training regimes.
Leap+Verify introduces both mechanisms: verify-then-accept prevents bad predictions from corrupting training, and regime conditioning restricts prediction to phases where trajectories are sufficiently regular.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Method</h2>

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Regime Detection via Activation Fingerprinting</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We detect training regimes by measuring the stability of the model’s internal representations.
At each checkpoint (every 50 training steps), we compute an <em id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">activation fingerprint</em>: the concatenated final hidden states produced by a fixed set of 100 probe sentences.
The cosine similarity between consecutive fingerprints serves as a proxy for the local Lyapunov exponent of the training trajectory.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Formally, let <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{a}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐚</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{a}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the activation fingerprint at step <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>.
We compute:</p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{t}=\frac{\mathbf{a}_{t}\cdot\mathbf{a}_{t-\Delta}}{\|\mathbf{a}_{t}\|\|\mathbf{a}_{t-\Delta}\|}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>𝐚</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>𝐚</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mi>𝐚</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mi>𝐚</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{t}=\frac{\mathbf{a}_{t}\cdot\mathbf{a}_{t-\Delta}}{\|\mathbf{a}_{t}\|\|\mathbf{a}_{t-\Delta}\|}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta=50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta=50</annotation></semantics></math> (the checkpoint interval).
We classify regimes using thresholds derived from initial training runs:</p>
<table id="S3.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{regime}(t)=\begin{cases}\text{stable}&amp;\text{if }s_{t}&gt;\tau_{\text{high}}\\
\text{chaotic}&amp;\text{if }s_{t}&lt;\tau_{\text{low}}\\
\text{transition}&amp;\text{otherwise}\end{cases}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>regime</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mtable columnspacing="5pt" displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mtext>stable</mtext></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mtext>if </mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><msub><mi>τ</mi><mtext>high</mtext></msub></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mtext>chaotic</mtext></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mtext>if </mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><msub><mi>τ</mi><mtext>low</mtext></msub></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mtext>transition</mtext></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mtext>otherwise</mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{regime}(t)=\begin{cases}\text{stable}&amp;\text{if }s_{t}&gt;\tau_{\text{high}}\\
\text{chaotic}&amp;\text{if }s_{t}&lt;\tau_{\text{low}}\\
\text{transition}&amp;\text{otherwise}\end{cases}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{\text{high}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>τ</mi><mtext>high</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{\text{high}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{\text{low}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>τ</mi><mtext>low</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{\text{low}}</annotation></semantics></math> are averaged across initial seeds.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The cosine similarity signal offers several advantages over alternatives.
Unlike Hessian eigenvalue computation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cohen et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, it requires only forward passes (no second-order gradients).
Unlike weight-space linear interpolation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Frankle et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, it operates in the representation space where functional similarity is more directly measured.
The probe set is fixed across all checkpoints, ensuring that changes in <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> reflect changes in the model’s representations rather than changes in input distribution.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Speculative Weight Prediction</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Given a checkpoint at step <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> with parameters <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, we predict parameters <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta_{t+K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>θ</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{t+K}</annotation></semantics></math> using three analytic predictors that exploit different trajectory properties:</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Momentum prediction.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Uses the exponential moving averages maintained by the Adam optimizer:</p>
<table id="S3.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\theta}_{t+K}^{\text{mom}}=\theta_{t}+K\cdot\frac{m_{t}}{\sqrt{v_{t}}+\epsilon}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>θ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mtext>mom</mtext></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mrow><msqrt><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></msqrt><mo>+</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\theta}_{t+K}^{\text{mom}}=\theta_{t}+K\cdot\frac{m_{t}}{\sqrt{v_{t}}+\epsilon}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> are Adam’s first and second moment estimates.
This extrapolates the current update direction at constant velocity.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Linear prediction.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Fits a line to two consecutive checkpoint states:</p>
<table id="S3.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\theta}_{t+K}^{\text{lin}}=\theta_{t}+\frac{K}{\Delta}(\theta_{t}-\theta_{t-\Delta})" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>θ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mtext>lin</mtext></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mfrac><mi>K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\theta}_{t+K}^{\text{lin}}=\theta_{t}+\frac{K}{\Delta}(\theta_{t}-\theta_{t-\Delta})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">This extrapolates the finite-difference velocity of the parameter trajectory.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Quadratic prediction.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Fits a parabola through three consecutive checkpoints:</p>
<table id="S3.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\theta}_{t+K}^{\text{quad}}=\theta_{t}+\frac{K}{\Delta}(\theta_{t}-\theta_{t-\Delta})+\frac{K(K-\Delta)}{2\Delta^{2}}(\theta_{t}-2\theta_{t-\Delta}+\theta_{t-2\Delta})" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>θ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mtext>quad</mtext></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mfrac><mi>K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></mrow></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\theta}_{t+K}^{\text{quad}}=\theta_{t}+\frac{K}{\Delta}(\theta_{t}-\theta_{t-\Delta})+\frac{K(K-\Delta)}{2\Delta^{2}}(\theta_{t}-2\theta_{t-\Delta}+\theta_{t-2\Delta})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">This captures curvature in the trajectory, accounting for acceleration/deceleration.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">After computing <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\theta}_{t+K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>θ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\theta}_{t+K}</annotation></semantics></math>, we load the predicted weights into the model and evaluate the validation loss <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{L}_{t+K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>L</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{L}_{t+K}</annotation></semantics></math>.
We compare this against the current validation loss <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> using three acceptance criteria:</p>
<ul id="S3.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Strict</span>: Accept if <math id="S3.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{L}_{t+K}&lt;L_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>L</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{L}_{t+K}&lt;L_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> (predicted improvement).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Adaptive</span>: Accept if <math id="S3.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{L}_{t+K}&lt;L_{t}+\sigma_{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>L</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>L</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{L}_{t+K}&lt;L_{t}+\sigma_{L}</annotation></semantics></math> (within one standard deviation of recent validation losses).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Proximity (pct)</span>: Accept if <math id="S3.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\hat{L}_{t+K}-L_{t}|&lt;\epsilon\cdot L_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>L</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\hat{L}_{t+K}-L_{t}|&lt;\epsilon\cdot L_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> (within a percentage of current loss).</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">If accepted, the model fast-forwards to step <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t+K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t+K</annotation></semantics></math>, skipping <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> gradient updates.
If rejected, training continues from step <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> with no modification—the prediction is purely speculative with no side effects.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Cascaded Prediction</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To test deeper speculation, we chain multiple predictions in sequence.
A cascade of depth <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math> with step size <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> applies prediction <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math> times, potentially advancing <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D\times K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D\times K</annotation></semantics></math> steps.
Each stage uses the predicted weights from the previous stage as its starting point.
Cascades are evaluated only from stable-regime checkpoints, where individual prediction accuracy is highest.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experimental Setup</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Models and Data</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate on two language models of different scale:</p>
<ul id="S4.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GPT-2 124M</span>: 12 layers, 768 hidden, 12 heads. Randomly initialized, trained from scratch.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Qwen 2.5-1.5B</span>: 28 layers, 1536 hidden, 12 heads. Randomly initialized from pretrained architecture config, trained from scratch.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Both models are trained on WikiText-103 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Merity et al., 2017</a>)</cite> with sequence length 256, using AdamW (<math id="S4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta=5\times 10^{-5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>η</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta=5\times 10^{-5}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta_{1}=0.9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>β</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.9</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta_{1}=0.9</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta_{2}=0.999" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>β</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.999</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta_{2}=0.999</annotation></semantics></math>, weight decay 0.01) with cosine learning rate schedule and 100-step warmup, for 2000 steps.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Evaluation Protocol</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For each model, we run five seeds (42–46) with identical hyperparameters.
Each run proceeds in three passes:</p>
<ol id="S4.I2" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S4.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Pass 1 (Training)</span>: Train for 2000 steps, saving checkpoints every 50 steps (40 checkpoints per seed). Record activation fingerprints and regime classifications.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Pass 2 (K-Sweep)</span>: For each non-chaotic checkpoint, evaluate all three predictors at <math id="S4.I2.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K\in\{5,10,25,50,75,100\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>25</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>50</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>75</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K\in\{5,10,25,50,75,100\}</annotation></semantics></math> with all three acceptance criteria. This yields up to <math id="S4.I2.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="40\times 3\times 6\times 3=2160" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>40</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>6</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2160</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">40\times 3\times 6\times 3=2160</annotation></semantics></math> evaluations per seed.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I2.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Pass 3 (Cascades)</span>: From stable-regime checkpoints, evaluate cascaded predictions with configurations <math id="S4.I2.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(D,K)\in\{(4,25),(2,50),(10,10)\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>D</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>25</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>50</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(D,K)\in\{(4,25),(2,50),(10,10)\}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Results</h2>

<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Training and Regime Detection</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S5.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 5.1 Training and Regime Detection ‣ 5 Results ‣ Leap+Verify: Regime-Adaptive Speculative Weight Predictionfor Accelerating Neural Network Training" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> summarizes the regime breakdown across both model scales.
Both models were trained for 2000 steps with checkpoints every 50 steps (40 checkpoints per seed).
Regime classification is based on activation-space cosine similarity (Section <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Regime Detection via Activation Fingerprinting ‣ 3 Method ‣ Leap+Verify: Regime-Adaptive Speculative Weight Predictionfor Accelerating Neural Network Training" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S5.T1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 1</span>: </span><span id="S5.T1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Regime breakdown by model scale (mean <math id="S5.T1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>±</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm</annotation></semantics></math> std across 5 seeds).

</tbody>
</table>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The regime distribution shifts dramatically with model scale.
GPT-2 124M spends 34% of training in stable regime and only 4% in chaotic, while Qwen 2.5-1.5B spends 64% in chaotic and reaches stable in only 0–2 of 40 checkpoints.
The first unknown checkpoint in each run reflects the initial state before consecutive fingerprints are available for similarity computation.
Cross-seed regime boundaries are highly consistent at both scales: the chaotic-to-transition boundary occurs within <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm 50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>±</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm 50</annotation></semantics></math> steps across all seeds.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">GPT-2 124M achieves a final validation loss of <math id="S5.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.616\pm 0.007" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.616</mn><mo>±</mo><mn>0.007</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.616\pm 0.007</annotation></semantics></math> across seeds.
Qwen 2.5-1.5B achieves <math id="S5.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.810\pm 0.019" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.810</mn><mo>±</mo><mn>0.019</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.810\pm 0.019</annotation></semantics></math> (range: 0.797–0.843), with training times of <math id="S5.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="34.9\pm 0.7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>34.9</mn><mo>±</mo><mn>0.7</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">34.9\pm 0.7</annotation></semantics></math> minutes per seed on A100 40GB with mixed precision.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>K-Sweep: Speculative Depth vs. Acceptance Rate</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Tables <a href="#S5.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 5.2 K-Sweep: Speculative Depth vs. Acceptance Rate ‣ 5 Results ‣ Leap+Verify: Regime-Adaptive Speculative Weight Predictionfor Accelerating Neural Network Training" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> and <a href="#S5.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 5.2 K-Sweep: Speculative Depth vs. Acceptance Rate ‣ 5 Results ‣ Leap+Verify: Regime-Adaptive Speculative Weight Predictionfor Accelerating Neural Network Training" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> present acceptance rates across prediction depth <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>, predictor type, and training regime.
Evaluations are performed only on non-chaotic checkpoints (transition + stable).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T2" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S5.T2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 2</span>: </span><span id="S5.T2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Strict acceptance rate (%) in transition regime: predicted loss must improve over current loss.
Values are mean <math id="S5.T2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>±</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm</annotation></semantics></math> std across 5 seeds.
<math id="S5.T2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> = total checkpoint evaluations across seeds.
</span></figcaption>
<table id="S5.T2.5" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="S5.T2.5.1" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S5.T2.5.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_r ltx_border_tt"><math id="S5.T2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math></th>
<td id="S5.T2.5.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt">Momentum</td>
<td id="S5.T2.5.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt">Linear</td>
<td id="S5.T2.5.1.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt">Quadratic</td></tr>
<tr id="S5.T2.5.2" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S5.T2.5.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_t" colspan="4"><span id="S5.T2.5.2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">GPT-2 124M — Transition regime</span></th></tr>
<tr id="S5.T2.5.3" class="ltx_tr">

</figure>
<div id="S5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Several patterns emerge across both scales.
First, momentum prediction achieves <span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">0% strict acceptance in transition regimes</span> at both scales.
In GPT-2’s stable regime, momentum achieves <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>10% strict and <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>17% proximity acceptance—non-zero but still far below finite-difference predictors, and reflecting the small fraction of checkpoints where momentum displacement happens to land in a favorable region.
Second, finite-difference predictors are substantially more effective in Qwen’s transition regime (37% strict at <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K{=}5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K{=}5</annotation></semantics></math>) than in GPT-2’s transition regime (9%)—larger models produce smoother trajectories in comparable regimes.
Third, GPT-2’s stable regime enables 22–24% strict acceptance at <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K{=}5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K{=}5</annotation></semantics></math>, better than its own transition regime but below Qwen’s transition performance.
Fourth, proximity-based acceptance reveals graceful degradation at both scales: <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>99–100% through <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K{=}5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K{=}5</annotation></semantics></math>, declining with <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>.
At 1.5B, proximity acceptance remains above 90% through <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K{=}25" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>25</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K{=}25</annotation></semantics></math>; at 124M, the decline is steeper (44% at <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K{=}25" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>25</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K{=}25</annotation></semantics></math> in transition, 75% in stable).</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The few Qwen stable-regime checkpoints (<math id="S5.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N{=}5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N{=}5</annotation></semantics></math> total across seeds) show 100% proximity acceptance through <math id="S5.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K{=}25" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>25</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K{=}25</annotation></semantics></math>, consistent with GPT-2’s stable-regime pattern.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.3 </span>The Universal Momentum Catastrophe</h3>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S5.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 5.3 The Universal Momentum Catastrophe ‣ 5 Results ‣ Leap+Verify: Regime-Adaptive Speculative Weight Predictionfor Accelerating Neural Network Training" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> quantifies the momentum predictor’s failure mode at 1.5B parameters.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S5.T4.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 4</span>: </span><span id="S5.T4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Momentum predictor failure at both model scales.
“Predicted loss” is the validation loss of the model with momentum-extrapolated weights; “Actual loss” is the current checkpoint’s validation loss.
Momentum catastrophe is universal—not scale-dependent.</span></figcaption>

<td id="S5.T4.5.3.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_r ltx_border_t"><math id="S5.T4.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="122\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>122</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">122\times</annotation></semantics></math></td>

<td id="S5.T4.5.3.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_t">0.82</td>
<td id="S5.T4.5.3.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_t"><math id="S5.T4.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="173\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>173</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">173\times</annotation></semantics></math></td></tr>

<td id="S5.T4.5.4.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right">0.82</td>
<td id="S5.T4.5.4.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right"><math id="S5.T4.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="305\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>305</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">305\times</annotation></semantics></math></td></tr>
<tr id="S5.T4.5.5" class="ltx_tr">

<tr id="S5.T4.5.7" class="ltx_tr">

</tbody>
</table>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The momentum catastrophe is universal across scales.
At 124M, predicted losses exceed actuals by <math id="S5.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="122\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>122</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">122\times</annotation></semantics></math> at <math id="S5.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K{=}5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K{=}5</annotation></semantics></math>, growing to <math id="S5.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="10{,}764\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>10,764</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10{,}764\times</annotation></semantics></math> at <math id="S5.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K{=}100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K{=}100</annotation></semantics></math>.
The GPT-2 ratios are actually <em id="S5.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">higher</em> than Qwen’s at large <math id="S5.SS3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> (<math id="S5.SS3.p2.m6" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="10{,}764\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>10,764</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10{,}764\times</annotation></semantics></math> vs. <math id="S5.SS3.p2.m7" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="3{,}009\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3,009</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3{,}009\times</annotation></semantics></math>): in absolute terms, GPT-2 momentum predictions reach 17,691 at <math id="S5.SS3.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K{=}100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K{=}100</annotation></semantics></math> vs. Qwen’s 2,468, likely reflecting GPT-2’s longer exposure to stable/transition regimes where momentum accumulates larger update magnitudes.
This is not a marginal degradation—it is a qualitative failure where the predicted weights lie far outside the region of the loss landscape explored during normal training.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">By contrast, linear prediction at <math id="S5.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K{=}5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K{=}5</annotation></semantics></math> produces predicted losses differing from actuals by <math id="S5.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&lt;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>&lt;</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&lt;</annotation></semantics></math>0.001 at both scales.
The <math id="S5.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10^{5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>5</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10^{5}</annotation></semantics></math>-fold difference between momentum and linear predictions at the same depth demonstrates that the choice of extrapolation basis (optimizer state vs. observed trajectory) is the critical design decision, not model scale.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">

<div id="S5.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">

Variance increases with <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>, as expected: longer predictions depend more on seed-specific trajectory details.
The quadratic predictor shows higher variance than linear at large <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>, reflecting its sensitivity to the curvature of individual trajectories.</p>
