</section>
<section id="S5.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.5 </span>Cascade Evaluation</h3>

<div id="S5.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Cascaded predictions (Section <a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3 Cascaded Prediction ‣ 3 Method ‣ Leap+Verify: Regime-Adaptive Speculative Weight Predictionfor Accelerating Neural Network Training" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>) were evaluated from stable-regime checkpoints.
At 1.5B scale, the scarcity of stable checkpoints (0–2 per seed) limits cascade evaluation.
For seed 46, Pass 3 cascades encountered an out-of-memory condition.
The limited cascade data available shows acceptance at short cascade depths (<math id="S5.SS5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D{=}2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D{=}2</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S5.SS5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K{=}10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K{=}10</annotation></semantics></math>) but rapid rejection at deeper cascades, consistent with error accumulation across prediction stages.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Discussion</h2>

<section id="S6.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.1 </span>The Universal Momentum Catastrophe</h3>

<div id="S6.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our most significant finding is that momentum-based weight prediction—extrapolating Adam’s exponential moving average of gradients—fails catastrophically at <em id="S6.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">every</em> model scale tested, not only at larger scales.
At 124M parameters, momentum-predicted losses exceed actuals by <math id="S6.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="122\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>122</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">122\times</annotation></semantics></math> at <math id="S6.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K{=}5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K{=}5</annotation></semantics></math>, growing to <math id="S6.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="10{,}764\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>10,764</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10{,}764\times</annotation></semantics></math> at <math id="S6.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K{=}100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K{=}100</annotation></semantics></math>.
At 1.5B parameters, the pattern is similar: <math id="S6.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="173\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>173</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">173\times</annotation></semantics></math> at <math id="S6.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K{=}5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K{=}5</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S6.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="3{,}009\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3,009</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3{,}009\times</annotation></semantics></math> at <math id="S6.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K{=}100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K{=}100</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">All three predictors operate in weight space, yet they differ in <em id="S6.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">how</em> they construct the extrapolation direction.
The momentum predictor uses Adam’s internal state (<math id="S6.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m_{t}/\sqrt{v_{t}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><msqrt><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m_{t}/\sqrt{v_{t}}</annotation></semantics></math>), which accumulates gradient information across the entire training history with exponential decay.
The linear and quadratic predictors use finite differences of <em id="S6.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">actually observed</em> checkpoint parameters (<math id="S6.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta_{t}-\theta_{t-\Delta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{t}-\theta_{t-\Delta}</annotation></semantics></math>), which implicitly capture the net effect of the learning rate schedule, gradient noise, and landscape curvature over the checkpoint interval.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The momentum predictor’s universal failure reflects norm explosion: the extrapolated direction <math id="S6.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K\cdot m_{t}/\sqrt{v_{t}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>/</mo><msqrt><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K\cdot m_{t}/\sqrt{v_{t}}</annotation></semantics></math> produces a displacement whose magnitude far exceeds the region of validity around the current point on the loss surface, regardless of model size.
The finite-difference predictors are inherently bounded by the actual step sizes taken during training, providing a natural regularization that momentum lacks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">This finding has practical implications for weight nowcasting methods like WNN <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jang and Han, 2023</a>)</cite> and NiNo <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Knyazev et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, which learn to predict in weight space.
Our results demonstrate that optimizer-state extrapolation is fundamentally unsuitable for speculative weight prediction, and that methods must use trajectory-bounded extrapolation—extrapolating from observed weight deltas rather than accumulated gradient moments.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.2 </span>Scale-Dependent Regime Distribution</h3>

<div id="S6.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The true scale-dependent finding is in the distribution of training regimes.
At 124M parameters, GPT-2 spends 34% of training in stable regime and only 4% in chaotic regime.
At 1.5B parameters, Qwen spends 64% in chaotic regime and barely reaches stable (2.5% of checkpoints).
Within comparable regimes, finite-difference predictors are actually <em id="S6.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">more accurate</em> at 1.5B: linear prediction achieves 37% strict acceptance in Qwen’s transition regime vs. 9% in GPT-2’s transition regime.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This suggests that larger models have smoother loss landscapes in their transition regimes—likely because more parameters enable more gradual representational changes—but spend far more of training in chaotic exploration.
The practical bottleneck for speculative weight prediction scales with model size not because prediction becomes harder, but because the training regime where prediction is viable becomes rarer.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.3 </span>Regime Detection as a Prerequisite for Prediction</h3>

<div id="S6.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The three-regime framework is essential, not merely convenient.
In chaotic regimes, no predictor achieves meaningful acceptance rates.
The regime detector prevents wasted computation by suppressing prediction attempts during these phases.
More importantly, the transition from chaotic to stable regimes occurs at remarkably consistent training steps across seeds (<math id="S6.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm 50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>±</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm 50</annotation></semantics></math> steps), suggesting that regime boundaries are properties of the optimization landscape rather than artifacts of random initialization.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.4 </span>Connection to ASC</h3>

<div id="S6.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The parallel between Leap+Verify and ASC <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Waterland et al., 2014</a>)</cite> runs deeper than analogy.
In ASC, the recognizer identifies states from which prediction is “tractable and useful”—precisely the role of our regime detector.
ASC’s predictors learn from observed trajectory structure, as do our weight extrapolators.
The trajectory cache stores verified state transitions; our acceptance criteria serve the same gatekeeping function.
Even the scaling behavior has parallels: ASC found that prediction accuracy varies by program structure, just as Leap+Verify finds that prediction accuracy varies by model scale.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The key difference is verification cost.
In ASC, verification requires executing the speculative segment and comparing end states—potentially as expensive as the original computation.
In Leap+Verify, verification requires only a single forward pass on held-out data, which is <math id="S6.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(1)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(1)</annotation></semantics></math> relative to the <math id="S6.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> gradient steps being predicted.
This asymmetry makes Leap+Verify’s verify-then-accept mechanism particularly favorable.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.5 </span>Limitations</h3>

<div id="S6.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Training was limited to 2000 steps on WikiText-103.
The Qwen 1.5B model barely reached stable regime within this budget (0–2 stable checkpoints out of 40), limiting our ability to evaluate predictors in the regime where they are most useful.
Longer training runs would likely yield more stable checkpoints and higher acceptance rates.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The regime thresholds (<math id="S6.SS5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{\text{high}},\tau_{\text{low}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>τ</mi><mtext>high</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>τ</mi><mtext>low</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{\text{high}},\tau_{\text{low}}</annotation></semantics></math>) were calibrated on GPT-2 124M and may require recalibration for larger models, where activation similarities tend to be higher overall.
An adaptive thresholding scheme would improve generality.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We did not evaluate ensemble collapse (dynamic reduction of multi-seed training runs based on detected convergence), which is a planned extension of the framework.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Weight prediction during training.</h4>

<div id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The concept of predicting future weights to accelerate training dates to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kamarthi and Pittner (1999)</a></cite>, who used Taylor series extrapolation.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sinha et al. (2017)</a></cite> trained neural predictors on weight histories.
Recent work has produced increasingly sophisticated methods: WNN <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jang and Han, 2023</a>)</cite> uses a learned nowcaster, NiNo <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Knyazev et al., 2025</a>)</cite> uses graph neural networks, and XGrad <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guan et al., 2024</a>)</cite> constructs mathematical future-weight relationships for specific optimizers.
PLP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anonymous, 2024</a>)</cite> applies linear prediction every 3 iterations.
All these methods apply predictions unconditionally; Leap+Verify introduces regime-conditional prediction with verify-then-accept.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Training dynamics.</h4>

<div id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cohen et al. (2021)</a></cite> identified edge-of-stability via Hessian eigenvalues.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Frankle et al. (2020)</a></cite> detected stable training via weight-space linear interpolation.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nanda et al. (2023)</a></cite> identified three mechanistic phases in grokking.
Our activation-space cosine similarity provides a computationally cheap alternative that operates in real time.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Loss landscape geometry.</h4>

<div id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al. (2018)</a></cite> introduced filter-normalized visualization.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Garipov et al. (2018)</a></cite> and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Draxler et al. (2018)</a></cite> established mode connectivity.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Keskar et al. (2017)</a></cite> linked batch size to basin sharpness.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Foret et al. (2021)</a></cite> operationalized flat-minima seeking via SAM.
These provide geometric context for why prediction difficulty varies by regime.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Adaptive optimization.</h4>

<div id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The Lookahead optimizer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2019</a>)</cite> maintains fast/slow weights with <math id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>-step lookahead, but always interpolates back (no acceptance criterion) and runs all <math id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> inner steps.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Smith (2017)</a></cite> showed cyclical learning rates implicitly traverse different curvature regimes.
RAdam <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2020</a>)</cite> automatically transitions between SGD-like and Adam-like behavior based on variance estimates—a single-signal regime detection for one transition.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Speculative execution.</h4>

<div id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Speculative decoding <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Leviathan et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2023</a>)</cite> and blockwise parallel decoding <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Stern et al., 2018</a>)</cite> provide the predict-then-verify template.
ASC <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Waterland et al., 2014</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Waterland et al., 2013</a>)</cite> generalizes this to arbitrary sequential computation via trajectory-based execution with learned predictors.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px6" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Dynamical systems in training.</h4>

<div id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Geiger et al. (2022)</a></cite> showed chaos is intrinsic to SGD.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tajanthan et al. (2022)</a></cite> connected Lyapunov exponents to Hessian eigenvalues.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Saxe et al. (2014)</a></cite> derived exact training dynamics for deep linear networks, revealing phase-transition-like behavior.
The Ensemble Kalman Filter literature <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Evensen, 1994</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2011</a>)</cite> provides analogies for regime-dependent ensemble behavior, where error growth concentrates in unstable regions.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S8" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">8 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We have introduced Leap+Verify, a framework for speculative weight prediction during neural network training that incorporates regime detection and verify-then-accept validation.
Our experiments reveal two key findings: (1) momentum-based weight prediction (optimizer-state extrapolation) fails catastrophically at <em id="S8.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">all</em> model scales (<math id="S8.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="100{-}10{,}000\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>100</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>10,000</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">100{-}10{,}000\times</annotation></semantics></math> loss inflation), while finite-difference extrapolation from observed weight trajectories succeeds with 9–37% strict acceptance depending on regime; and (2) the distribution of training regimes shifts dramatically with scale—larger models spend far more time in chaotic regimes where no predictor is viable.
Together, these findings suggest that weight-space prediction methods must use trajectory-bounded extrapolation rather than optimizer-state extrapolation, and that the primary challenge at scale is <em id="S8.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">regime availability</em>, not predictor accuracy.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The regime detection framework—classifying training into chaotic, transition, and stable phases using activation cosine similarity—provides a computationally cheap signal that generalizes the edge-of-stability and linear mode connectivity observations in prior work.
The verify-then-accept mechanism, transplanted from speculative decoding and ASC, ensures that bad predictions have zero cost: rejected leaps leave the training trajectory unmodified.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Future work will extend the framework in three directions: (1) adaptive regime thresholds that recalibrate with model scale, (2) ensemble collapse—dynamically reducing multi-seed training runs when regime detection indicates cross-seed convergence, and (3) evaluation at larger scales (2.7B, 7B) to map the full predictor hierarchy.</p>
</div>
</section>
